newsitem.title: NORWAY: FOCUS-Storebrand, Christiania mull future alone.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Storebrand, Christiania mull future alone.

text.p: Shares in Norway's largest insurer, Storebrand ASA, fell six percent on Friday after shareholders blocked a bid to merge with Christiania Bank og Kreditkasse ASA.
Analysts said Storebrand looked to have lost the most from the failed proposal, while it appeared to be business as usual at Christiania Bank.

Storebrand's stock slid almost nine percent just after the opening of the Oslo bourse to an intraday low at 43.00 crowns. By 1315 GMT it had recovered to 44.30, 5.9 percent down in turnover of 34 million crowns. Christiania Bank was 1.22 percent up at 24.80 crowns.

Analysts said the two major challenges facing Storbrand were widening the life insurance distribution network in Norway and cost reduction and capital structure in the non-life business. The latter would require a cross-border Scandinavian solution.

"It's difficult to see what alternatives are open to Storebrand now. It needs a partner but it has no money to buy anything. Maybe a solution would be to split life and non-life and offer the latter to international investors," one analyst said.
Some said the company would likely undergo a period of management uncertainty following the board's defeat.

More than 62 percent of voters opted for the merger, which was largely blocked by two major shareholders -- conglomerate Orkla ASA and private investor Kjell Inge Roekke -- holding 10 percent each. A two-thirds majority of shareholders was required to pass the deal.

"There was a big power game between Roekke, Orkla and the Storebrand management. Roekke and Orkla won, the question is will they be satisfied to leave alone or do they now have plans," commented one observer.
For Christiania Bank domestic analysts said there was little opportunity or need for further consolidation in the commercial banking sector.
A merger between the two largest banks -- Den norske Bank (DnB) and Christiania Bank -- is currently politically difficult given the state's majority ownership in the two.
Such a tie-up could also open up opportunities for Swedish and Danish competitors as Norwegian businesses prefer to share their financial affairs with at least two banks, analysts said.
International players saw a broader structure in the longer term.

"Christiania will certainly have to look elsewhere. The consolidation that has happened in Sweden has put additional pressure on the sector in Norway," said Matthew Czepliewicz, European banking analyst at Salomon Brothers in London.

One analyst said international investors may have been turned off the Norwegian banking scene following a series of messy takeover struggles involving DnB, Fokus Bank, savings bank Sparebankgruppen and niche mortgage lender BNbank. The apparent power play between between Storebrand, Roekke and Orkla had not helped.

"The problem in Norway is this 10 percent rule. That means forming alliances and positioning yourself if you want to make an impact," he said, referring to Norwegian regulations allowing any single investor to hold a maxmium 10 percent stake in a financial institution.
